BOOK ENTRY
The transgression of the law — Scripture's own definition: “sin is the transgression of the law”; where no law is, there is no transgression, and by the law is the knowledge of sin.
[.opposite]Opposite: Righteousness.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(1 John 3:4; Rom 4:15; 3:20; 7:7) · see Grace, Mercy & the Gift, ch. 24

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
1 John 3:4 — Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law.
Romans 4:15 — Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression.
Romans 3:20 — Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.
Romans 7:7 — What shall we say then? Is the law sin? God forbid. Nay, I had not known sin, but by the law: for I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet.

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the Scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” that the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, Scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very Scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the Scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/24-path-to-salvation.adoc

Ask any Christian what grace is, and the answer comes back in a formula: unmerited favor — getting what you don't deserve.
Ask about mercy and the usual answer is: not getting the punishment you do deserve.
Ask about the gift of God: salvation — free; a gift can only be received, never earned.

None of these is wrong.
Every one of them is half-true.

The formulas tell you what grace and mercy cost you — nothing — and stop before telling you what they do.
Scripture goes further, and it starts higher: both words are written into God's own Name, proclaimed to Moses in the cleft of the rock — “merciful and gracious… keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty.”
Forgiveness and the unforgiven stand in the same sentence of the same Name.
The formulas are missing a clause — something decides which side of that sentence a man stands on — and this chapter recovers the three words to find it.

Begin where the formula is right.
Grace moves before any deserving:

But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

The word's first appearance in Scripture is the same shape: “Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD” (Genesis 6:8) — favor toward one man in a world already condemned.
Unmerited is exactly right.

Now watch what the formula leaves out.
When John says “grace and truth came by Jesus Christ” (John 1:17), he is quoting the Name-proclamation — “abundant in goodness and truth” — the pair God announced at Sinai now walking in person.
Grace never travels alone; its companion is the truth, and “thy law is the truth” (Psalm 119:142).
Paul gives grace its job description:

For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;

Grace arrives free, and then it goes to work — a tutor, not an exemption.
The one verse always quoted against this — “ye are not under the law, but under grace” (Romans 6:14) — Paul guards himself, in the next breath: “What then? shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid” (Romans 6:15); to yield to sin is to be sin's servant, “or of obedience unto righteousness” (Romans 6:16).
Not under the law's condemnation; never out from under its instruction — grace is the teacher, not the end of school.
Scripture even names the counterfeit: “ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness” (Jude 4) — grace re-sold as license.
The test between them is simple: real grace produces sober, righteous, godly living; the counterfeit produces permission.

The Hebrew beneath most of the Bible's “mercy” is chesed — covenant loyalty, steadfast love — and Moses sets it in its frame:

Know therefore that the LORD thy God, he is God, the faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations;

“Covenant and mercy” travel as one phrase; mercy lives inside the covenant, kept toward its keepers — “the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him… to such as keep his covenant” (Psalm 103:17-18).
Hebrew's other mercy-word says how deep it runs: racham, compassion, shares its letters with rechem, the womb — “Can a woman forget her sucking child?… yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee” (Isaiah 49:15).
Mercy is womb-love: loyal because of what you are to Him, not because of what you did.

How is it obtained?
Scripture answers in mechanics, not mood:

He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.

Confess — and forsake.
Isaiah adds the turning: “Let the wicked forsake his way… and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon” (Isaiah 55:7).
Ezekiel writes the clause that should astonish more than it does:

If the wicked restore the pledge, give again that he had robbed, walk in the statutes of life, without committing iniquity; he shall surely live, he shall not die.
None of his sins that he hath committed shall be mentioned unto him: he hath done that which is lawful and right; he shall surely live.

Turn, do right, restore what can be restored — and the ledger is wiped: none of it so much as mentioned.
Repentance in Scripture has four parts, not three: confess the sin; plead guilty — “against thee, thee only, have I sinned… that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest” (Psalm 51:4); change the heart to desire what is good; and make restitution where restitution can be made, as Zacchaeus did fourfold (Luke 19:8).

Jesus told mercy as accounting:

Therefore is the kingdom of heaven likened unto a certain king, which would take account of his servants.
And when he had begun to reckon, one was brought unto him, which owed him ten thousand talents.
But forasmuch as he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold… The servant therefore fell down… saying, Lord, have patience with me, and I will pay thee all.
Then the lord of that servant was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt…
O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?
And his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors, till he should pay all that was due unto him.
So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.

Here mercy is shown in full.
The debt is real and unpayable — ten thousand talents, a sum no servant sees in a lifetime.
The cancellation is total, and it is granted on asking: “because thou desiredst me.”
Paul names the instrument: “blotting out the handwriting that was against us… nailing it to his cross” (Colossians 2:14) — the debt-note itself, canceled and nailed up where every debtor can read it.

The canceled note has terms on the back.
The pardoned man who will not pardon gets his debt reinstated — “so likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you.”
This is no isolated hard saying; it is the standing rule of the kingdom: “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7); “if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses” (Matthew 6:15); “he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy” (James 2:13).
Mercy in Scripture is not a one-way transaction; it is a circuit — received, then required.
Jesus files it where the formulas never look: among “the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith” (Matthew 23:23) — mercy is law-content, a thing commanded and done: “do justly, and love mercy, and walk humbly with thy God” (Micah 6:8).
The Name-proclamation's two poles now close: He keeps mercy for thousands and forgives — the confessing, forsaking, forgiving; He will by no means clear the guilty — the covering, defiant, unmerciful.
The clause the formulas were missing is repentance, and mercy practiced.

One verse holds the whole economy:

For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

The contrast is the verse's own structure: opsōnia, a soldier's wages — earned, owed, paid in full — against charisma, the grace-gift.
Death is the one thing every sinner has fully earned; eternal life is the one thing no man ever will.
Jesus closes the earning door in a sentence:

Does he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded him?
I think not.
So likewise you, when you have done all those things which you are commanded, say, ‘We are unprofitable servants.
We have done what was our duty to do.’

Perfect obedience earns nothing; it was already owed.
As servants, we have nothing our Creator did not give us first; we owe Him our very life, and every sin grows the debt — and the first rule of getting out of a hole is to stop digging.
Obedience cannot pay the old debt; only the blood cancels that.
What obedience does is stop the new one.

Paul refuses works in exactly this ledger's terms, and he defines the working he refuses: “Now to him that worketh is the reward reckoned not of grace, but of debt” (Romans 4:4) — work done to put God in debt, obedience tendered as a ransom-price.
Hebrew carries the wage inside the word: one noun, pe'ullah, is both work and wages, and Isaiah announces the coming LORD with it — “behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him” (Isaiah 40:10) — the very line Revelation quotes as the judgment formula: “behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be” (Revelation 22:12).
Deeds carry their pay — which is exactly why they cannot buy back a forfeited life whose wage is already earned.
What Paul never refuses is the doing of the law: “the doers of the law shall be justified” (Romans 2:13); “do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law” (Romans 3:31).
The working he refuses is wage-logic; the walk he commands is obedience.

For by grace you have been saved through faith.
And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.

Both hands in one passage: not of works — no man earns it; for good works — no man receives it and stands idle.
The gift, like the wedding garment, is granted, then worn.

Grace and mercy meet at a specific address:

Seeing then that we have a great high priest… Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.

The throne of grace is where mercy is obtained — the two words the formulas separate work one office, and the office is the law's own.
It is the law that establishes a High Priest, the sacrifice he presents, and the sins his atonement covers — and the law divides sin in two:

The priest shall make atonement before the LORD for the person who commits an error when he sins unintentionally, making atonement for him so that he may be forgiven…
But the person who does anything wrong willfully and defiantly… that one is blaspheming the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from among his people.

Unintentional sin has an altar; defiant sin refuses the altar's terms.
Hebrews carries the same division into the new covenant:

For if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment…
Of how much worse punishment, do you suppose, will he be thought worthy who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, counted the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified a common thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace?

The truth is the law, so willful sin after receiving it is lawbreaking with the eyes open — and the most open-eyed form of all is the claim that there is no law to break, that it was done away, that “Jesus has paid the price for you not following it.”
That claim does not plead the blood; it counts the blood a common thing.
Jesus prescribes the escape to a fallen assembly, and it is measured in works resumed: “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Revelation 2:5) — repentance is not a feeling; it is what is resumed.
The healed are dismissed with the same charge — “go, and sin no more, lest a worse thing come upon you” (John 5:14; 8:11) — and since sin is lawlessness, “sin no more” means go and keep the law.

If willful sin after knowledge is worse than never knowing, who then can be saved?
Paul answers with his own struggle:

For the good that I will to do, I do not do; but the evil I will not to do, that I practice…
For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man.
But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members.
O wretched man that I am!
Who will deliver me from this body of death?
I thank God — through Jesus Christ our Lord!
So then, with the mind I myself serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.

Paul's own position is clear: he calls the law good and delights in it in the inward man, while the flesh he drags behind him keeps breaking it.
That is not the defiant sinner of Numbers 15; it is the unintentional one, at war, confessing, covered by the High Priest — the publican's whole prayer: “God be merciful to me a sinner” (Luke 18:13).
The man who agrees with the law and loses battles against his flesh has an altar.
The man who denies the law has refused it.

That if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.

Confessing Jesus as Lord means He is your Master — and He does nothing but what the Father commanded: “I have come down from heaven, not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me” (John 6:38).
Call Him Master, and His Father's law becomes your desire; deny the law, and you have denied the Lordship in the confession — the word emptied while the mouth still moves.

The familiar three-step path holds, but each step stands on the law it forgot.
Admit you are a sinner — you cannot, without the law that defines sin.
Believe He paid for your sin on the cross — you cannot, without the law that demands the sacrifice, establishes the High Priest, and prophesies the Messiah who meets both.
Confess Him Lord — you cannot, without submitting to obey Him.

Is perfect obedience possible?
Not in the flesh.
Is perfect obedience required for salvation?
No. But a mind and heart of obedience is.
Many say “Lord, Lord,” while their hearts say there are no laws, because I am forgiven — a reckless driver claiming there are no rules of the road because someone has paid his tickets.
The paid ticket is mercy; the gratitude that slows down is grace doing its teaching; the license kept is the gift.
He who does the will of the Father enters (Matthew 7:21) — not earning the kingdom, but refusing to insult the Spirit of the grace that brought him to its gate.

The servant who means to keep His commands exactly will want them exactly as they were written — which raises a question this book has been leaning on since the Introduction, where one word was read two ways: what, precisely, did the prophets write?
That question opens the next part of this book.
